hook.text: The Sun blasts charged particles at 1.6 million km/h in every direction. That stream is the solar wind.

buildup.text: It carries protons and electrons past every planet, reaching far beyond Pluto into deep space.

discovery.text: Earth's magnetic field deflects most of the solar wind. Without it, our atmosphere would be stripped away.

twist.text: Mars lost its magnetic field 4 billion years ago. The solar wind stripped its atmosphere, leaving it barren.

climax.text: The heliopause is where the solar wind meets interstellar space. Voyager 1 crossed it in 2012.

punchline.text: The Sun exhales. Our magnetic field is the umbrella.

quiz.question: Why did Mars lose most of its atmosphere?
options: Its magnetic field died, and the solar wind stripped the atmosphere away
A giant asteroid impact blew the atmosphere into space
Mars was always too small to hold any atmosphere

details.summary: The solar wind is a continuous stream of charged particles (mostly protons and electrons) flowing outward from the Sun at 400-800 km/s. It fills the entire solar system, shapes planetary magnetospheres, creates comet tails that always point away from the Sun, and defines the heliosphere's boundary…
details.whyItMatters: The solar wind shapes the space environment of every planet. It strips atmospheres from unprotected worlds (like Mars), creates auroras on Earth, and defines the boundary where our Sun's influence ends and interstellar space begins.
takeaways: It's a continuous stream of charged particles from the Sun
It flows at 400-800 km/s throughout the solar system
It creates comet tails and shapes planetary magnetospheres

faq.question: Where does the solar wind stop?
faq.answer: At the heliopause — roughly 120 astronomical units from the Sun — where solar wind pressure balances interstellar medium pressure. Voyager 1 crossed this boundary in 2012 and Voyager 2 in 2018, becoming the first human-made objects to enter interstellar space.

faq.question: How does the solar wind create auroras?
faq.answer: Charged solar wind particles are funneled by Earth's magnetic field toward the poles. When they collide with atmospheric gases (oxygen and nitrogen), those gases emit light — green and red from oxygen, blue and purple from nitrogen. This creates the shimmering aurora borealis and aurora australis.
